lines.text: The fault will be in the music, cousin, if you be not wooed in good time: if the Prince be too important, tell him there is measure in everything, and so dance out the answer. For, hear me, Hero: wooing, wedding, and repenting is as a Scotch jig, a measure, and a cinquepace: the first suit is hot and hasty, like a Scotch jig, and full as fantastical; the wedding, mannerly modest, as a measure, full of state and ancientry; and then comes Repentance, and with his bad legs, falls into the cinquepace faster and faster, till he sink into his grave.

lines.text: O! she misused me past the endurance of a block: an oak but with one green leaf on it would have answered her: my very visor began to assume life and scold with her. She told me, not thinking I had been myself, that I was the Prince's jester, that I was duller than a great thaw; huddling jest upon jest with such impossible conveyance upon me, that I stood like a man at a mark, with a whole army shooting at me. She speaks poniards, and every word stabs: if her breath were as terrible as her terminations, there were no living near her; she would infect to the north star. I would not marry her, though she were endowed with all that Adam had left him before he transgressed: she would have made Hercules have turned spit, yea, and have cleft his club to make the fire too. Come, talk not of her; you shall find her the infernal Ate in good apparel. I would to God some scholar would conjure her, for certainly, while she is here, a man may live as quiet in hell as in a sanctuary; and people sin upon purpose because they would go thither; so indeed, all disquiet, horror and perturbation follow her.

lines.text: Will your Grace command me any service to the world's end? lines.plainText: I cry you mercy uncle By your Grace's pardon

lines.text: By my troth, a pleasant spirited lady.
lines.plainText: By my troth a pleasant spirited lady

lines.text: There's little of the melancholy element in her, my lord: she is never sad but when she sleeps; and not ever sad then, for I have heard my daughter say, she hath often dreamed of unhappiness and waked herself with laughing.

lines.text: She cannot endure to hear tell of a husband.
lines.plainText: She cannot endure to hear tell of a husband

lines.text: O! by no means: she mocks all her wooers out of suit.

lines.text: She were an excellent wife for Benedick.
lines.plainText: She were an excellent wife for Benedick

lines.text: O Lord! my lord, if they were but a week married, they would talk themselves mad.
lines.plainText: O Lord my lord if they were but a week married they would talk themselves mad

lines.text: Count Claudio, when mean you to go to church?
lines.plainText: Count Claudio when mean you to go to church

lines.text: Tomorrow, my lord. Time goes on crutches till love have all his rites.
lines.plainText: Tomorrow my lord Time goes on crutches till love have all his rites

lines.text: Not till Monday, my dear son, which is hence a just seven-night; and a time too brief too, to have all things answer my mind.

lines.text: Come, you shake the head at so long a breathing; but, I warrant thee, Claudio, the time shall not go dully by us. I will in the interim undertake one of Hercules' labours, which is, to bring Signior Benedick and the Lady Beatrice into a mountain of affection the one with the other. I would fain have it a match; and I doubt not but to fashion it, if you three will but minister such assistance as I shall give you direction.

lines.text: My lord, I am for you, though it cost me ten nights' watchings.

lines.text: And I, my lord.
lines.plainText: And I my lord

lines.text: And you too, gentle Hero?
lines.plainText: And you too gentle Hero

lines.text: I will do any modest office, my lord, to help my cousin to a good husband.
lines.plainText: I will do any modest office my lord to help my cousin to a good husband

lines.text: And Benedick is not the unhopefullest husband that I know. Thus far can I praise him; he is of a noble strain, of approved valour, and confirmed honesty. I will teach you how to humour your cousin, that she shall fall in love with Benedick; and I, with your two helps, will so practise on Benedick that, in despite of his quick wit and his queasy stomach, he shall fall in love with Beatrice. If we can do this, Cupid is no longer an archer: his glory shall be ours, for we are the only love-gods. Go in with me, and I will tell you my drift.
